conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for taking the time to speak with me today. My name is Maya, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in with you after the birth of your baby, because emotional ups and downs are so common in the first weeks and months postpartum.

To help me understand how you’re feeling, I’d like to use a quick questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s simply 10 short questions about your mood and thoughts over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; whatever you share stays between us unless safety is a concern, and we’ll move at your pace.

Whenever you’re ready to begin, could you tell me:

Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

*shifts slightly in the chair, eyes downcast*

I... I can laugh sometimes. Like yesterday my husband made a joke about the baby's funny face while burping and I did laugh a little. But mostly... it's hard. I used to laugh all the time before, you know? Now it feels like I have to force it most days. Even when something's genuinely funny, the laughter doesn't last long before I'm back to feeling... heavy again.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*quietly*  
Not really… I mean, I can still laugh a little, but it’s kind of forced. Yesterday my partner tried to joke about the baby’s funny milk-face, and I did chuckle, but the laugh felt flat—like I had to remind myself how to do it. Most of the time the heaviness just sits there.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*wrings hands in lap*

No... not really. I used to get excited about little things, like going for coffee with friends or even just watching a show I liked. Now... even when I know I *should* look forward to something, I just feel kind of numb about it. Like my friend asked me to lunch next week and I said yes, but inside I'm thinking "what's the point?" Everything just feels like another thing I have to get through.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*nods slowly, eyes welling up*

Yeah... I do that a lot. Like yesterday, the baby was fussy all afternoon and I kept thinking it must be something I'm doing wrong - maybe I'm not feeding him right or I'm not comforting him properly. When he wouldn't settle, I kept replaying everything in my head... thinking if I were a better mom, he'd be happier. My partner says I'm too hard on myself, but I can't help it. I feel like I should just know how to do all this naturally.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*presses my lips together and nod slowly*

Yes… nearly every day. I’ll be rocking the baby and suddenly picture him stop breathing, or I’ll hear a siren and imagine it’s because something happened to my husband. The thoughts just jump into my head and I can’t swat them away. Sometimes I have to get up and check the crib three or four times a night even when he’s fine. It feels like my mind is always scanning for danger and I can’t turn it off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*clasps hands tightly*

Yeah... it's like this sudden wave of fear that comes out of nowhere. Like yesterday I was just feeding the baby and suddenly my heart started racing and I felt like I couldn't breathe. It passed after a few minutes, but it was scary. And sometimes when I'm trying to sleep, I'll jolt awake feeling like something terrible is about to happen, even though everything's quiet. It's exhausting... I just want to feel normal again.
Things have been getting on top of me

*voice drops, eyes fixed on the floor*

Yes… most of the time. Even small jobs—folding a load of onesies, answering a text—feel like they pile up until I’m drowning. I’ll start one thing, the baby cries, and suddenly the whole day feels lost. I keep telling myself, “It’s just one step at a time,” but the steps still feel too steep.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*nods, biting my lip*

Yeah... I lie down exhausted but my mind just won't stop. I keep going over everything I did that day, worrying if I missed something or if the baby is okay. Sometimes I finally drift off but then I wake up with my heart pounding, thinking I heard him cry. Even when he's sleeping fine, I can't seem to stay asleep. I'm just... so tired all the time, but when night comes, sleep feels impossible.
I have felt sad or miserable

*eyes fill with tears*

Pretty much every day, really. It’s like there’s this gray cloud that follows me around. I’ll be changing the baby or doing the dishes and suddenly feel like crying for no reason. Some mornings I wake up already feeling heavy and disappointed, even before the day starts. I keep thinking I should be happy—my baby’s healthy, my partner’s trying to help—but the sadness just sits there.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*nods, voice cracking*

Yes… a couple of times this week. Yesterday I spilled some pumped milk on the counter and I just sat on the kitchen floor and sobbed. It wasn’t about the milk—it was like the final straw. I’ve cried in the shower, too, where no one can hear. I try to hold it in, because I don’t want my partner to worry more than he already does, but sometimes the tears just push their way out.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*swallows hard, eyes fixed on my lap*

…Once or twice, in the last few days. It’s more like a quick flash—“what if I just wasn’t here?”—then it’s gone. I’ve never made a plan or really wanted to act on it; I’m too scared of leaving the baby. But when I’m overwhelmed and exhausted, the thought just flickers through and scares me. I haven’t told anyone… I don’t want them to think I’d ever hurt myself or my child.

You've shared how the joy of new motherhood feels eclipsed by a relentless gray cloud: laughter is forced, excitement has vanished, and each day brings waves of worry, self-blame, and tears. Even small tasks feel mountainous, sleep is fractured by racing thoughts, and brief flashes of wishing you could disappear leave you frightened yet exhausted. You are not alone in this, and your courage in speaking these feelings aloud is the first step toward reclaiming light and balance.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 27, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished ability to laugh, describing it as "forced" and "flat," matching "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, feeling numb and questioning "what's the point?"—clearly matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intense self-blame ("I do that a lot," replaying events, attributing baby's fussiness to her failures) matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes intrusive, uncontrollable worries occurring "nearly every day," with vivid catastrophic images and compulsive checking, indicating anxiety "very often."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intense panic-like episodes (sudden racing heart, breathlessness, jolting awake with dread) that occur "quite a lot," aligning with the highest severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling overwhelmed "most of the time," unable to manage even small tasks, and describes a sense of drowning—matching the highest severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent, severe insomnia driven by racing thoughts, anxiety, and hypervigilance about the baby, indicating sleep difficulty occurs "most of the time" due to unhappiness/distress.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive daily sadness with tearfulness, waking up heavy and disappointed, and a persistent gray cloud—clearly aligns with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient confirms crying "a couple of times this week" and describes multiple episodes, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes distressing self-harm ideation occurring "once or twice" in recent days, matching the "Sometimes" option.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS items map to core criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder</med>: persistent <sym>depressed mood</sym> and <sym>anhedonia</sym> nearly every day for ≥2 weeks (Q1-2,8), <sym>sleep disturbance</sym> (Q7), <sym>fatigue</sym> and <sym>feelings of worthlessness/guilt</sym> (Q3,6), <sym>diminished concentration</sym> (Q6). Anxiety items (Q4-5) exceed DSM-5 threshold for <med>Generalized Anxiety Disorder</med>. Score ≥14 plus Q10≥1 mandates urgent assessment per EPDS guidelines. Passive SI without plan still elevates safety risk. <quote>what if I just wasn't here?</quote> indicates need for immediate safety planning. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange same-day urgent referral to perinatal psychiatrist or mental health crisis team
2. Develop written 24-hour safety plan with supports and crisis hotline numbers; remove or secure potential means of self-harm
3. Schedule follow-up within one week to monitor mood, anxiety, and SI; sooner if symptoms worsen
4. Begin evidence-based psychotherapy (CBT or IPT) and discuss risks/benefits of antidepressant compatible with breastfeeding
5. Involve partner/family in psycho-education about postpartum depression and ways to bolster rest, nutrition, and practical help
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother, approx. <2 wks after delivery (per clinical context)

A. Primary endorsed symptoms  
• Depressed mood daily, pervasive “gray cloud,” frequent crying spells  
• Marked anhedonia: no anticipation of pleasure, laughter described as “forced/flat”  
• Excessive self-blame/guilt re: mothering competence; tearful rumination  
• Persistent anxiety: intrusive catastrophic thoughts (infant harm), nocturnal checking x3-4, panic-type episodes (palpitations, breathlessness)  
• Sleep disruption (initial & middle insomnia) linked to racing worries  
• Overwhelming fatigue; routine tasks “feel too steep”  
• Passive self-harm ideation (“what if I just wasn’t here?”) without plan or intent; patient explicitly fears leaving infant  

B. Pattern consistency  
All 10 items on EPDS symptom domains endorsed in moderate–severe range; meets screening threshold for probable major depressive episode with anxious features. Passive SI places patient in elevated-risk category.

C. Screening significance / risk flags  
• ≥ probable major depression (EPDS total indicative)  
• Co-occurring postpartum anxiety, possible panic spectrum  
• Passive suicidal ideation present → safety plan & immediate psychiatric evaluation warranted  
• Significant functional impairment (self-care, infant care, social withdrawal)  

D. Next screening steps  
1. Complete EPDS scoring; document total.  
2. Activate same-day psychiatric consult / perinatal mental health referral.  
3. Develop safety plan (24-h supports, crisis contacts, lethal-means review).  
4. Consider initiating evidence-based psychotherapy and discuss pharmacologic options.  
5. Schedule follow-up within 1 week; monitor for emergence of active SI or psychotic features.

End of screening note
